name: Protect Your Home from Wildfire — Fire Resistant Vegetation and Landscaping
publisher: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Forestry, Community Forestry Program
scaleNotes: The 56 printed taxa in the source's Alaska firewise-landscape examples map to recommend with its placement-and-maintenance condition. Four genus examples under Characteristics of plants that ignite and burn readily map to avoid. Accepted-name reconciliation collapses the 60 entries to 58 evidence owners.
notes: All printed scientific identities were retained at their printed rank. Source spelling damage and obsolete combinations were reconciled only through explicit corrections and exact GBIF matches; source spellings remain in the parser and evidence claims. The taxon-free "Ferns, native and non-native" row was held. The guide gives no test method or citations, so tier remains unset and lineage unknown. The current official 74,657-byte download was reopened on 2026-08-26. Official PDF SHA-256: 68afb4eedbffab6e049e7c771326c1e9bd7a4f071ab2a754d256178b0fc7755e.

name: Firewise Landscaping for Woodland Homes
publisher: Alabama Forestry Commission
scaleNotes: The booklet separates suggested trees, shrubs, and groundcovers from four fire-prone plants to avoid within 30 feet of the house. Suggested rows map to recommend and the explicit avoid rows map to avoid.
notes: The five-page Alabama Forestry Commission PDF was recovered from its 2002-09-13 Wayback capture after disappearing from the live site in 2003. The final printed page carries the Alabama Forestry Commission imprint, publication code AFC-FP-04, and year 1999; the PDF metadata is dated 2002-02-25. Thirty-one printed occurrences resolve to 27 exact GBIF owners; the repeated Acer genus row is represented once. Three rows are held rather than broadened: one schema-inexpressible form and two named cultivars. Printed errors corrected transparently for matching are Celtis occidentallis -> Celtis occidentalis, Llex -> Ilex, and Magnolia stellara -> Magnolia stellata. name: Recommended Acceptable Fire Resistive Plant Species
publisher: Anaheim Fire & Rescue
scaleNotes: Binary acceptable list.
notes: Derives from older State of California agency lists (the CA agency tree rooted in the LA Arboretum program). Southern California climate context; corroborates flammability claims, never regional suitability for the PNW.

name: Fire Resistant and Retardant Plants
publisher: Australian Plants Society Victoria (Neil Marriott)
scaleNotes: Two classes: fire-resistant (52 plants that will not burn in the face of continued flame) and fire-retardant (92 plants that resist the first wave of a bushfire but may burn once dried out). Both classes map to recommend, with the class preserved verbatim on each row.
notes: Member-experience curation from burnt properties plus a foliage flare-up test — closer to field observation than list-copying, and independent of the CFA lineage. Carries the Sweet Pittosporum delisting: previously fire-retardant, now noted as highly flammable once dried, agreeing with Tasmania's X-coded row.

name: Best Practices for Fire Resistant Landscaping
publisher: City of Ashland
scaleNotes: Recommendations defer to PNW 590; the prohibited-species list (AMC 9.04.022, adopted by resolution) is original regulatory content with legal force.
notes: Prohibited list rows are adoption/regulatory evidence; recommendation rows are PNW 590-derivative.

name: Prohibited Flammable Plants (Ashland Municipal Code 9.04)
publisher: City of Ashland, Oregon (Fire & Rescue / Weed Abatement)
scaleNotes: A municipal prohibition list: the named trees, shrubs, and grasses may not be newly planted or allowed to propagate within 30 feet of any structure (AMC 9.04), with canopy- and shrub-spacing standards under AMC 18.3.10.100. Verdict map: prohibited = avoid. Starred taxa may receive dwarf or prostrate-variety exceptions only with fire department approval, placement beyond five feet, and ordinance-compliant spacing.
notes: Regulatory evidence, not a flammability measurement — an adopted ordinance that corroborates avoid verdicts. Assigned to the pnw590 tree conservatively: an Oregon ordinance in the PNW-guidance sphere has not been demonstrated independent of that lineage, and independence must be shown, never assumed and matters directly to the Oregon audience. Mostly genus-level rows (all pines, all junipers, all cedars), which attach to genus records and leave species-level lab evidence undisturbed. The source's historical Rosmarinus spp. row is held rather than projected onto the much broader modern Salvia genus.

name: Firewise Landscaping in North Carolina (E05-44596)
publisher: NC State University / NC Cooperative Extension + USFWS (Bardon, Van Druten)
scaleNotes: Four-tier flammability rating (Low / Medium / High / Extreme) for ~200 North Carolina natives, by growth form with habitat columns. Verdict map: Low = recommend, Medium = mixed, High and Extreme = avoid.
notes: The root of all NC ratings, including (near-certainly) the Plant Toolbox, whose signature four-value scale this document originated. National Fire Plan funded. Agency copy retired; town mirrors persist.

name: Evaluation of the flammability of trees and shrubs used in green barriers in southern Brazil
publisher: USDA Forest Service (Batista, Biondi, Tetto et al.; Universidade Federal do Paraná)
scaleNotes: The paper applies Valette's 0-5 epiradiator flammability scale to live leaves and thin branches. Verdict map: 0-1 (non/low flammability) = recommend; 2-3 (moderately flammable/flammable) = mixed; 4-5 (highly/extremely flammable) = avoid.
notes: Complete English full text and Table 2 are publicly hosted by the USDA Forest Service. All five exact species are represented. Batista, Biondi, Tetto, and Kovalsyki recur in the UFPR green-barrier program, so this and its Brazilian companion papers share one ufpr-cortinas-tree vote. Use of Valette's method alone does not merge this new dataset with Valette's INRA lineage.

name: Flammability evaluation of Ligustrum lucidum for potential use in fuelbreaks
publisher: Revista Brasileira de Ciências Agrárias (Batista & Biondi; UFPR)
scaleNotes: Verdicts follow the authors' explicit interpretation of replicated 1 m2 burn plots: Ligustrum lucidum = low flammability/recommend; Pinus taeda = high-flammability control/avoid. Rate of spread, flame height, and fire intensity remain in the evidence claims rather than being remapped.
notes: The complete CC-BY full text and result tables are publicly available. Both exact measured taxa are represented. Batista's UFPR laboratory, method program, and later-paper authorship connect this experiment to the ufpr-cortinas-tree, so it enriches that lineage without adding a vote.

name: Flammability of native understory species in pine flatwood and hardwood hammock ecosystems
publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Behm, Duryea, Long, Zipperer)
scaleNotes: The paper rejects a single composite flammability index and instead names four taxa as the most flammable, one as the least flammable, and describes wax myrtle's measured characteristics as moderate. Verdict map: the named most-flammable group = avoid; the named least-flammable taxon = recommend; every other measured taxon = mixed. No threshold or score is inferred.
notes: Species-level fuel structure, biomass, moisture, volatile-solids, and energy measurements for ten unique taxa sampled as twelve ecosystem-by-species groups. The author-uploaded article is publicly readable in full. Behm, Long, and Zipperer overlap the later Long 2006 whole-plant study, so both papers remain one ufifas-srs-tree lineage vote.

name: Canberra Plant Selector — fire-retardant attribute
publisher: ACT Government / Everyday Climate Choices
scaleNotes: The public selector exposes a Fire Retardant Yes/No filter and repeats the selected attribute on each result card. Only Yes rows map to recommend. No is absence of the positive selector attribute and is not converted to an avoid verdict.
notes: The live 2026-08-25 tool reports 259 total plants and 131 Fire Retardant: Yes plants, replacing the registry's stale estimate of 342. All 22 filtered result pages were captured at one request per second. Named cultivars were collapsed only where the printed label also states a species; genus-only hybrid/cultivar labels, two authorless homonyms, an unrepresentable subspecies row, and a variety collapsed by GBIF were held. Of 131 printed Yes rows, 122 exact GBIF owners are represented (72 existing records enriched and 50 records created); nine rows are retained in the ledger as held.

name: Comportamento do fogo em espécies nativas da Caatinga na região geográfica imediata de Patos-PB
publisher: Ciência Florestal, Universidade Federal de Santa Maria
scaleNotes: Ten species were compared in three replicated outdoor 1 m² burns. Tables 6-9 report ignition attempts/time, flame height, combustibility index, spread rate, fire intensity, and severity. Only Cnidoscolus quercifolius and Aristida adscensionis receive explicit overall flammability conclusions.
notes: Leaves and branches no more than 0.7 cm in diameter were air-dried for 30 days; each treatment used 9 kg of fuel. Cnidoscolus quercifolius did not sustain flame spread, so it is absent from the later metric tables and its fire intensity is described as zero. publisher: Colorado Department of Agriculture and Colorado Secretary of State
scaleNotes: List A is a statewide eradication designation. List B is statewide listed with management objectives that can vary by county or rule plan. List C supports local integrated management and education.

The snapshot is text-extractable and is parsed only within asserted section boundaries with exact expected counts. The source states no reusable upstream license; derived FireApproved rows remain CC BY 4.0.

name: Safer Gardens: Plant Flammability & Planning for Fire
publisher: Lesley Corbett / Australian Scholarly Publishing
scaleNotes: The book synthesizes low, moderate, and high plant flammability findings, preserving conflicts among primary studies. notes: Eleven exact public findings were ingested. The website publishes a 500-plus plant name index, but names alone are not ratings and were not converted to evidence. The omitted full table remains a documented access gap. publisher: CSIRO
scaleNotes: The guide is almost entirely design-, maintenance-, and trait-based. Its one explicit taxon-level suitability statement names Grevillea at genus rank; that statement maps to recommend. Generic advice to choose low-flammability species was not converted into taxon evidence.

name: Ignition-Resistant Landscape Plants (Fact Sheet 6.305)
publisher: Colorado State University Extension / Colorado State Forest Service (Wildfire Mitigation Series)
scaleNotes: 114 ignition-resistant plants scored 7.5-10 on the 0-10 ignitability scale, with the fact sheet's own doctrine that only plants scoring 8, 9, or 10 belong in defensible-space zones 1 and 2. Verdict map: 8-10 = recommend, 7.5 = mixed (below the source's own zone-1-2 bar). The sheet credits "the Idaho materials" as the basis of the scoring, so rows whose scores duplicate the Idaho Firewise master database resolve to that root.
notes: The 2025 revision replaces the unscored FireWise Plant Materials lists of the 2001-2010 editions (Wayback captures archived for edition-diffing). A recommend-side list only; it condemns nothing. Exact replay audited 2026-08-25: all 114 rows resolve to existing GBIF owners, using nine documented exact corrections. Seventy-eight score-identical rows resolve to Idaho via original; 36 rows remain CSU-original. The hardened parser creates no records and every row carries full table placement and lineage. name: Flammability of some companion species in cork oak forests
publisher: Annals of Forest Science (Dehane, Hernando, Guijarro & Madrigal)
scaleNotes: K-means classifications of fresh and oven-dried fuels differ. The paper's abstract explicitly identifies Calicotome spinosa, Tetraclinis articulata, Juniperus oxycedrus, and Pinus halepensis as highly flammable. Verdict map: this explicit overall high group = avoid; all other measured taxa = mixed. No recommend verdict is inferred from a favorable fresh-only cluster.
notes: The complete article is publicly archived in HAL. All ten exact species are represented. Fresh twigs with foliage and paired oven-dried samples were tested by mass-loss calorimeter. Hernando, Guijarro, and Madrigal place this in the INIA Madrid fire-lab program already represented by Ganteaume; the Algerian samples are new data but share one inia-madrid-tree vote.

name: Delaware 3 DE Admin. Code 806 Invasive Plant and Plant Watch Lists
publisher: Delaware Department of Agriculture
scaleNotes: The current regulation names 39 Invasive Plant List taxa and one Plant Watch List taxon. Chapter 29 restricts import, export, purchase, sale, transport, distribution, and propagation of viable listed material. Invasive-list activities require the Secretary's prior written approval for the statute's disposal, control, research, education, or bounded export purposes. The Watch row instead requires the published tag, label, or sign. Four May 2026 additions have department enforcement dates in 2028 or 2029.
notes: The May 2026 final order adopts the March 2026 regulatory text unchanged and makes it effective ten days after publication. The current DDA page supplies the clean complete list, identifies 35 invasive-list rows with enforcement in effect, two additions with enforcement beginning May 1, 2028, two additions beginning May 1, 2029, and twelve current named cultivar exemptions. Chapter 29 supplies the activity and prior-written-approval boundaries. Regulation 806 states that cultivar exemptions are conditional and subject to revocation. Legal status, ecological invasion, and fire performance remain separate dimensions.

name: Possible land management uses of common cypress to reduce wildfire initiation risk: a laboratory study
publisher: Elsevier / Journal of Environmental Management (IPSP-CNR and INIA-CIFOR)
scaleNotes: Component-level study of Cupressus sempervirens var. horizontalis live crown and dead litter. The authors report relative resistance to ignition and low crown/litter ignitability, while requiring multiple methods to characterize sustainability, combustibility, and consumability. Both rows map to mixed; no overall low-flammability class is inferred.
notes: Tier 1 bench-scale laboratory study using mass-loss calorimetry, epiradiator, and oxygen bomb methods. The selected-variety cypress-barrier application is framed as a promising complementary tool needing further study. Evidence remains variety-, part-, moisture-, and placement-specific and does not roll up to the species or genus.

name: Combustion characteristics of north-eastern USA vegetation tested in the cone calorimeter
publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Dibble, White, Lebow)
scaleNotes: The paper reports several cone-calorimeter measurements and warns that their rankings are not interchangeable. Verdicts therefore use only the abstract's author-named effective-heat-of-combustion extremes: taxa named high = avoid; taxa named low = recommend; every other measured taxon = mixed. This is a map of the conditioned foliage-and-twig result, not a whole-plant claim.
notes: Public full text is hosted by the USDA Forest Service. Thirty-six identified vascular species and one genus-rank Vitis row are represented. Cynanchum cf. louiseae remains held because a cf. determination is not a genus rating; three bryophytes and one lichen remain held because the current directory schema has no defensible nonvascular plant form. Dibble and White overlap the Forest Products Laboratory cone-calorimeter program represented by White et al. 2002 and Weise et al. 2005, so this is one usfs-fpl-cone-tree vote.

name: Landscaping for Wildfire Defensible Space in Northeastern Minnesota (Firewise)
publisher: Dovetail Partners (Ely, MN; supported by The Nature Conservancy / USDA Forest Service PERFACT agreement)
scaleNotes: Table 2 rates 38 wildfire-resistant, non-invasive plants low or moderate flammability using the UF/IFAS Circular 1453 methodology (Behm, Long, Monroe, Randall, Zipperer, Hermansen-Baez 2004), with the document's own placement mapping — low-flammability plants may be planted 3 to 30 feet from a building, moderate ones beyond 30 feet. Verdict map: low = recommend, moderate = mixed.
notes: The only rated Minnesota list; a clean application of the Florida flammability key to northeastern Minnesota natives, with growing-condition columns (form, soil moisture, sun, hardiness zones). The document's boreal-tree flammability table (Table 1) is attributed to Manitoba's FireSmart program and is not part of this source's own ratings. The pinned input is 4,647,325 bytes; SHA-256: d2ae26cd78f2246f54435421d6914900cea71475bb70249d1447accf945bb042.

name: Landscaping to Reduce Wildfire Risk: South Florida Edition
publisher: Florida Forest Service
scaleNotes: Narrative hazard callouts rather than a ranked plant table. The guide calls five named invasive plants extremely flammable, flags grape vine as a fire concern, calls palmetto highly combustible, and describes condition-dependent fire spread on cabbage palm.
notes: Written and designed for the Florida Forest Service by Melissa Yunas and Victor Hill. The guide links Firewise and University of Florida resources but gives no claim-level provenance or rating method, so its evidence lineage remains unknown. The eight represented owners preserve only taxonomic precision supported by the printed common or genus names. The pinned official PDF is 4,425,484 bytes. Official PDF SHA-256: 883a3538a62612580f8e4758df34283d91d11b04b5260702138c3c0edf316a89.

name: Low Flammability Plants directory
publisher: Fire and Emergency New Zealand (plant flammability testing at Lincoln University)
scaleNotes: Seven-level flammability classification (Very low / Low / Low-moderate / Moderate / Moderate-high / High / Very high) across 402 species, grounded in shoot-flammability testing at Lincoln University (the Curran-group "plant barbecue" program). Verdict map: very low, low, and low-moderate = recommend (the directory calls low and low-moderate species ideal for planting); moderate and moderate-high = mixed; high and very high = avoid. A separate list of twelve high-flammability environmental weeds (2024 Department of Conservation list) maps to avoid.
notes: The deepest lab-derived official plant flammability directory anywhere, and the corpus's first Southern Hemisphere lab chain. Website content is CC-BY-NC-ND, so only uncopyrightable facts are extracted — species names, classifications, and poisonous/weed flags — with attribution in text. Accessed via FENZ's checkitsalright.nz property; origin column is NZ-relative.

name: Selective Shrub Management to Preserve Mediterranean Forests and Reduce the Risk of Fire
publisher: MDPI Fire / University of Évora and Instituto Politécnico de Viana do Castelo
scaleNotes: Table 2 marks 16 native genera Control in mainland Portugal fuel-management bands. Control maps to avoid only within that placement. The 18 Preserve genera are not mapped to recommend because the decision also incorporates succession, conservation value, and protected status.
notes: Perspective grounded in phytosociology, literature synthesis, and the authors' 2017 post-fire observation. Fine-textured heliophilous shrubs are prioritized for selective control. The stable registry slug predates source inspection; the actual authors are Raposo, Pinto Gomes, and Nunes, not Fernandes.

name: Fire-Resistant Plants Common to Marin County
publisher: Fire Safe Marin
scaleNotes: The publication separates named fire-resistant plants from a shorter fire-prone list. It also identifies plants suitable for hedges. Fire Safe Marin says placement, spacing, irrigation, and removal of dead material remain necessary; it does not describe an experimental rating method.
notes: The source remains tierless because its selection lineage is only partly documented. Its rows publish Marin's curation and conflicts without creating independent Tier 1 support in the derived rating.

name: FireSmart BC Plant Program — fire-resistant plant chart
publisher: FireSmart BC
scaleNotes: Binary FireSmart-approved chart of 290 plants across eight growth-form categories, each with a Home Ignition Zone suitability (intermediate 10-30 m / extended 30-100 m / extended and beyond) or a needs-more-research flag. Verdict map: approved = recommend.
notes: Tier 2 compiled corroboration: FireSmart BC's chart substantially republishes the PNW-590 species set for BC, so rows landing on records that already carry pnw-590 evidence resolve to that root and add no independence. Zone suitability is preserved as placement guidance; needs-more-research flags travel as claims.

name: FireWise Plants offer colorful choices for Fire Safe Gardens
publisher: NFPA Firewise Communities
scaleNotes: The page presents its 19-row table as a short representation of Firewise trees, shrubs, and groundcovers homeowners can choose. Every table row maps to recommend. Its unscientific generic avoid examples are held separately.
notes: Nineteen exact GBIF species owners were admitted from the visually audited table. Printed Juglans cincerea and Rhus copallinum errors were corrected transparently to Juglans cinerea and Rhus copallina. The generic warning to avoid pine, cedar, and juniper was not converted because it supplies no scientific names and cedar is taxonomically ambiguous. The page contains no byline or Arkansas statement; its filename suggests Arkansas, but the captured 2006 NFPA plant-list index does not include it. State coverage remains deliberately untyped until an archived index or authoring record directly establishes that scope. publisher: NFPA Firewise Communities
scaleNotes: The single-page list describes every table row as a fire-resistive plant that can be used in landscaping. Each exact taxon row maps to recommend; the page provides no comparative score or avoid category.

Nine obvious printed misspellings are preserved in verdictRaw and corrected transparently for matching. publisher: Dorset Heaths Partnership / Firewise UK / University of Exeter wildFIRE Lab
scaleNotes: University of Exeter wildFIRE Lab testing is published as green, amber, and red classes. Verdict map: green = recommend; amber = mixed; red = avoid. The leaflet defines red dry material as capable of flames over 2.5 m.
notes: The two-page public leaflet and its visual class columns were verified. Eleven unambiguously identified species/cultivars were ingested. Seventeen entries labelled only by a genus or ambiguous common name were excluded rather than assigned a taxon. This is one exeter-wildfire-tree lab program vote.

publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service

The guide says most listed plants require some irrigation during dry summers and that even fire-resistant plants can burn if not maintained in a healthy condition. publisher: Dryad / Global Ecology and Biogeography
scaleNotes: FLAMITS stores 19,972 numeric observations across 40 harmonized variables and five flammability dimensions. name: Flammability of some ornamental species in wildland-urban interfaces in southeastern France
publisher: Environmental Management (Ganteaume, Jappiot, Lampin, Guijarro, Hernando)
scaleNotes: The hierarchical analysis assigns poorly flammable, not very flammable, moderately flammable, highly flammable, and extremely flammable clusters. Guijarro and Hernando overlap the INIA Madrid fire-lab papers, so this source conservatively shares the inia-madrid-tree vote. It uses Valette's published epiradiator protocol and scale, but has different authors and a new ornamental dataset, so protocol reuse alone does not merge it with Valette 1990.

publisher: Diputació de Barcelona and CREAF

notes: Eighteen exact taxon labels are admitted from the printed panel: 14 maintain/less-flammable rows and four remove/more-flammable rows. Quercus, Tamarix, Pinus, Cupressus, Cistus, and Erica remain genus-rank because the panel prints sp. rather than a species. Pistacia terebintus is retained in verdictRaw while its transparent spelling correction resolves to Pistacia terebinthus. name: Guía de pirojardinería — guía práctica de jardinería adaptada a la prevención de incendios forestales

scaleNotes: The 289 species fiches use five printed suitability verdicts: muy recomendada, recomendada, desaconsejada, muy desaconsejada, and prohibida. name: Virginia 2VAC5-317 Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 Noxious Weeds
publisher: Virginia Board of Agriculture and Consumer Services
scaleNotes: The current regulation names three Tier 1, seven Tier 2, and sixteen Tier 3 noxious weeds. The tiers describe presence and feasibility of eradication or suppression; they do not create three uniform sales classes. Section 30 prohibits movement of a regulated article unless it is accompanied by a valid certificate or permit. Section 10 defines a regulated article as a listed weed or an article carrying or capable of carrying one. It separately defines a certificate as commissioner-issued or authorized documentation of noncontamination and a permit as movement to restricted destinations for limited handling, utilization, processing, or scientific purposes.
notes: The official Virginia Register final record, VA.R. Doc. No. R21-6889, filed May 15, 2024 and effective July 4, 2024, adds one Tier 2 and eleven Tier 3 species and prints the same 26-row list as the current code page. The current Section 10 definitions and Section 30 movement rule supply the legal effect, including the distinct certificate and permit meanings under the rule's either-or operating path. The amendment date identifies the current list edition; it is not assigned as the original designation date of every older row. Legal status, ecological invasion, seed regulation, and fire performance remain separate dimensions.
